title: Taking in side seams, checking quality and job cards

say: Taking in side seams, checking quality, and using job cards.
This is the video for module three of Basic Tailoring and Garment Repair.
Many people own clothes that fit almost right. A gown loose at the waist, or a skirt that has become tight. Taking in and letting out side seams are the most requested fit alterations.

say: Here is the calculation that matters most. Suppose you move a stitching line 1 cm inward.

panel.heading: Every seam counts twice
items: Front loses 1 cm, back loses 1 cm
Two side seams: 4 cm smaller in total

say: You remove 1 cm from the front piece, and 1 cm from the back piece, at that seam.

panel.heading: Every seam counts twice
items: Front loses 1 cm, back loses 1 cm
Two side seams: 4 cm smaller in total

say: So the garment becomes 2 cm smaller at that one seam.

panel.heading: Every seam counts twice
items: Front loses 1 cm, back loses 1 cm
Two side seams: 4 cm smaller in total

say: With two side seams, it becomes 4 cm smaller in total. So for two side seams, divide the total reduction you want by four.
Always alter both sides by the same amount, so the side seams stay at the sides of the body.

panel.rule: Two side seams: divide the total reduction by four

say: For example, Ruth brings Adaeze an ankara gown that is 6 cm too big at the waist and 4 cm too big at the hip. The bust fits.
At the waist, 6 divided by four is 1.5 cm per seam.

panel.heading: Taking in Ruth's ankara gown
items: Waist 6 cm too big: 1.5 cm per seam
Hip 4 cm too big: 1 cm per seam
Taper back to 0 cm, 10 cm above waist
Baste and do a second fitting

say: At the hip, 4 divided by four is 1 cm per seam. She marks the new line on both sides.

say: She tapers the line back to nothing about 10 cm above the waist, so the bust is untouched. A smooth taper over about 8 to 10 cm hides the change.

say: She bastes, which means tacking with loose running stitch, and does a second fitting. The fit is right.

say: Only then does she machine stitch, finish the edges with zigzag and press. Do not cut away extra allowance until the customer has tried it on. Fabric cannot be added back.

say: To let a garment out, first unpick a small section inside and measure the seam allowance. If it is 2 cm, you can usually let out about 1 cm per seam and keep 1 cm to hold it. Across two side seams, that is up to 4 cm more room.

panel.heading: Check the allowance first
left: Let out up to about 1 cm
Keep 1 cm to hold the seam

say: On dark or shiny fabric, the old stitch holes may still show. Test on the inside, and tell the customer honestly before you start.

panel.heading: Check the allowance first
left: Let out up to about 1 cm
Keep 1 cm to hold the seam

say: Customers judge you by small details. Puckering means the seam wrinkles. Check your threading, try a new fine needle, and let the machine move the fabric instead of pulling it.

cards.d: Check threading, use a new fine needle, and let the feed dogs move the fabric. Do not pull.
Change the needle. Use a ballpoint needle for knits. Check the flat side faces the right way.
Measure each leg, pin more closely, and press before stitching.

say: Skipped stitches usually mean the needle. Change it, and use a ballpoint needle for knits. Most stitch faults come from the needle or threading, not the tension dial.

Measure each leg, pin more closely, and press before stitching.

say: An uneven hem means one leg was not measured. For example, Grace checks four pairs of school trousers, finds one leg 1 cm longer, and re-hems it before the parent arrives.

say: Check every job against this list. Even, balanced stitches. Straight, locked seams with no puckering. Both legs or sleeves matching within about half a centimetre.
Raw edges finished. Buttons and zips opening and closing smoothly ten times. Loose threads trimmed, chalk removed, and the garment pressed. Press means lift and set down the iron, not slide it.

panel.heading: Your quality checklist
items: Both sides match within about 0.5 cm

say: Most quarrels come from unclear instructions, missed dates and price. A job card prevents them. Write the job number, date, and the customer's name and phone.

panel.heading: What goes on a job card
items: Job number, date in, name and phone

say: Write the work agreed and the measurements.

panel.heading: What goes on a job card
items: Job number, date in, name and phone

say: Note any existing damage, and tell the customer.

panel.heading: What goes on a job card
items: Job number, date in, name and phone

say: Agree the price before starting, and record the deposit and balance. Before releasing a garment, confirm the money has arrived in your own bank or wallet app, not from the customer's phone screen. Fake alerts are common.

panel.heading: What goes on a job card
items: Job number, date in, name and phone

say: Give a realistic collection date. Keep measurements private, and ask before taking or posting any photo.

panel.heading: What goes on a job card

say: Your practice: take in an old shirt or dress, audit three of your pieces against the checklist, fill in two job cards, and write a short weekly summary.
